Beállítom A Ukrainian proposal involving several countries, a memorandum of understanding about a reservoir near Hungary’s border with Ukraine, late-night messaging between Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and MOL Chairman-CEO Zsolt Hernádi, and the Hungarian PM commenting under the Ukrainian Foreign Minister’s social media post are all part of the diplomatic back-and-forth between Ukraine and Hungary, which has rapidly escalated in recent days. The full context is still unclear, but at the center of it all is Volodymyr Zelensky’s regional initiative, which the Ukrainian president claimed Hungary was a member of. But on Monday, Magyar clearly stated that this is not the case. According to the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, however, this should not be interpreted as a rejection of regional cooperation or of constructive relations with Ukraine. No nameplate, no flag The brief history of the Carpathian Eight (Seven?) began last Friday with Zelensky's announcement of a new cooperation initiative between Ukraine and seven (six?) European countries, as well as the EU as a whole. This initiative aims to strengthen economic cooperation among the member states in several areas. As reported by Zelensky himself and the Ukrainian press, the first summit took place on Friday. Writing about the initiative, the Ukrainian President noted that this is the first time such a summit-which brings together all the states of the Carpathian region-has been held in Ukraine, specifically in that part of the Carpathians. According to him, the Carpathian Eight (C8)—which he said includes Hungary—is a movement that brings member countries closer together. “The goal is to significantly expand cooperation in the areas of security, energy, logistics, and economy across borders, as well as to provide substantial support to our communities,” Zelensky wrote about the C8 . The Ukrainian President first welcomed the leaders and representatives of the Carpathian Eight publicly on social media. In another post, he then specifically named Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary, and, of course, Ukraine. However, the photo shared on his X-account only features the leaders and politicians of six countries. From left to right: Czech politician Jiří Drahoš; Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk; Romanian President Nicușor Dan; Olena Zelenska, the wife of the Ukrainian president; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky; Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić; and Christine Schwarz-Fuchs, President of the Austrian Federal Council. In other words, member states were represented at varying levels, and there was no one from Slovakia or Hungary present at this initial gathering. In response to our inquiry on Friday as to whether anyone was representing Hungary, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the head of the Hungarian Embassy in Kyiv was attending the event on behalf of Hungary. In a video subsequently shared by Zelensky, it was evident that representatives of the member states were seated at a table listening to the Ukrainian president’s welcoming remarks. However, there were only seven nameplates visible here: those of the six politicians mentioned earlier, who were in attendance, and that of Marek Eštók, the Slovak State Secretary for European Affairs and Foreign Affairs, who was also visible in subsequent photos and videos. Of the flags of the alleged member states in the hall, only the Hungarian flag was missing. On Saturday, Zelensky again mentioned Hungary among the members, although it was quite striking that when he listed the countries in his video, there was only one country-Hungary-for which they were unable to show the face of a single participant. In his subsequent reports on the event, the Ukrainian President consistently wrote about the leaders of the C8. Incidentally, when he addressed the press, there were only politicians from six other countries seated next to him. “During the Russian aggression, the Carpathian macroregion became one of the most reliable foundations of our defense. This is about a strength that exists today and will continue to exist in the future,” wrote the Ukrainian president. The storage facility rattled everything Then some news broke on Sunday which, in light of the radical erosion of Ukrainian–Hungarian relations during the Orbán governments, seemed unusual at first glance. According to this, Hungary's oil giant, Mol and the Ukrainian company Naftohaz had signed a memorandum of understanding at the C8 summit about building fuel storage facilities near the Hungarian-Ukrainian border, on Hungarian territory, to serve the Ukrainian market. The head of the Ukrainian energy company, who announced the memorandum of understanding, made no secret of the fact that this would be advantageous for them due to the war. Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting director of Naftogaz wrote that diversifying supply routes and building additional storage facilities in areas not affected by Russia’s continuous attacks on their fuel supply infrastructure would contribute to the stability of the entire market. “The implementation of this joint project will ensure the reliability of fuel supplies in the long term, and not only for Ukrainian consumers,” stated the Ukrainian side. Both Fidesz and the KDNP (the Christian Democratic Party, Fidesz’s former coalition partner) immediately jumped on the news, with several of their politicians speaking out on the subject on Facebook on Sunday. Fidesz’s Barbara Hegedűs posed a series of questions about the additional risks and asked why this would be good for Hungary. Olivér Hortay, also of Fidesz, called it a bad decision. “In the Russian-Ukrainian war, the parties are attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, so with this investment, our country is putting itself in the crosshairs,” he said. The KDNP, meanwhile, wrote that “because of Russian drone attacks, Ukraine is having a strategic crude oil storage facility" built in Hungary”. Late-night texting, and the Carpathian Eight minus one Finally, the subject was also raised in parliament on Monday. It was first brought up by Bence Rétvári. The KDNP faction leader pointed out that Hungarian voters found out about “the Ukrainians installing dangerous infrastructure in Hungary” from Ukrainian-language news reports. Fidesz faction leader János Bóka also spoke about the memorandum signed by MOL and the Ukrainian company Naftogaz, which he said was drafted “on the sidelines” of the Carpathian Eight summit. “Did the government know about this? If not, why not? Was there any security analysis conducted?” he asked. In his response, Péter Magyar noted that the opposition parties—i.e. Fidesz and the KDNP—had drawn attention to an issue involving a storage facility “announced by Mol, which may or may never be built near Hungary’s border with Ukraine” but had omitted to mention a few details. The Prime Minister said that he had had a lengthy telephone conversation with Mol Chairman and CEO Zsolt Hernádi on Sunday night, and it turned out that negotiations about this storage facility had begun during the previous government’s term. “He said that they began negotiations with the authorization from the Orbán government, just as you also supplied weapons—you just denied it,” Magyar said. The PM added that Hernádi was not appointed by the current, but by the previous government. The Prime Minister said that his phone conversation with the Chairman and CEO of MOL was about the fact that the current Hungarian government had not received any information about MOL having begun negotiations with the Ukrainian side—and, incidentally, with the Americans as well-with the authorization of the previous government about the possible construction of such a storage facility. Péter Magyar also touched on the “Carpathian Eight” announced by Zelensky on Friday: he wanted to know whether the opposition representatives had noticed that the Prime Minister of Poland, the President of Serbia, and high-ranking representatives from several other countries were present at the Carpathian Eight meeting, but there was no one from Hungary. “I’d like to set the record straight here as well, because I heard from the Ukrainian press that Hungary is a member of this ‘Carpathian Eight.’ It is not a member. We were invited, and we had good reason not to go,” said Péter Magyar. The Prime Minister also stated that he had made it clear to Hernádi that there would be no reservoir built on the Hungarian–Ukrainian border—or anywhere else—under the Tisza government. According to Magyar, Mol had, in fact, only signed a “memorandum of understanding,” and the company’s press release makes it clear that this is merely a theoretical possibility. He concluded by reading aloud from the text message from the exchange he had with Mol’s chairman and CEO—specifically, the message he had sent to Hernádi at the end of their phone conversation. “The way Mol is conducting itself is completely unacceptable. We will communicate this formally as well. From now on, we expect—I expect—Mol to treat the Hungarian state as a 25 percent shareholder in the company,” the Prime Minister quoted from his own text message. He added that they would have to wait and see what the consequences of all this would be. During Monday’s debate in Parliament, the issue of the “Carpathian Eight” and the reservoir came up several times. Magyar repeatedly stated that Hernádi is one of “your people,” i.e. of Fidesz–KDNP. “If he did something wrong, then feel free to hold him accountable.” The Prime Minister reiterated that Hungary is not a member of the Carpathian Eight. “And if it ever does join, it will certainly announce it,” he said. Gas storage is a profitable business, but Mol understood the message Mol subsequently backtracked, noting that the studies and negotiations are still at a very early stage. “This is a preparatory step for the project, which is not binding. But the government’s position is clear, and we understand it” György Bacsa, Group Chief Strategic officer of Mol said at Tuesday’s G7 Paradigma conference. In the hydrocarbons market (whether it be gas, oil, or products), extraction, production (refining), transportation, and storage are all opportunities for business. In Mol’s case, the storage services it provides to several countries are a particularly lucrative business. The fact that this has now become a topic of political discussion is a bit like the Field Eryngo (or White Devil) plant, which, when it withers, detaches from the ground at its base, and the wind rolls it across the plains like a ball, thereby scattering its seeds. As the wind blows carries the plant, it sometimes separates other plants or gets them tangled with others; it is such a politically not-so-sensitive activity that has now come under greater scrutiny. From a purely economic perspective, a Hungarian–Ukrainian storage agreement could be a profitable venture because there is a so-called product pipeline running from Tiszaújváros towards Ukraine. Larger pipelines running between Hungary and Ukraine, such as the “Friendship” oil pipeline or the “Brotherhood” gas pipeline are better-known, but these smaller pipelines rarely make the news. The Eastern Product Pipeline, which used to run from Tiszaújváros all the way to Samara, Russia, is still usable for inexpensive and safe transportation towards the Ukrainian section. Its history dates back to 1956, when Soviet troops entered Hungary, and Moscow decided to use a pipeline to supply fuel to the Soviet army, which was supposed to be stationed in Hungary temporarily, but ended up staying for a very long time. Construction lasted from 1957 to 1966. From then on, fuel could be transported to Hungary via the pipeline from the east, partly for military and partly for commercial purposes. It later became possible to connect various refineries and fuel depots located within the Soviet Union to it. More recently, the direction of transport has been reversed; the pipeline that passes above Kyiv is now capable of transporting diesel, for example, from Hungary to Ukraine. A major advantage of the pipeline is that it runs underground, making it harder for Russia to attack it than, for example, rail shipments, and the use of the existing infrastructure naturally also offered cost advantages. Hungary has continued to supply diesel to Ukraine via the pipeline throughout the war, and there were no attacks against it. Hungary would be able to ship more diesel—as much as 50,000 to 60,000 metric tons per month—but it cannot process enough. A storage facility would help keep up with the demand, and building one would take at least two to three years, even after the final decision has been made. Once the Danube Refinery returns to operating at full capacity, Hungary would be able to export more, and if the war is over by then, this would be a major competitive advantage. Magyar's message to the Ukrainian Foreign Minister on social media Following Péter Magyar’s statements in Parliament, we contacted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to ask why they did not wish to join the C8 initiative and, why it was that despite this, the head of the Hungarian Embassy in Kyiv attended Friday’s meeting. We also inquired as to the basis on which President Zelensky announced that Hungary was part of the initiative and with whom he had consulted on this matter on behalf of the Hungarian government. In addition, we contacted the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs to ask what negotiations they were aware of on the subject, and we also inquired on what basis Ukrainian President Zelensky claimed that Hungary was also a member of the initiative. “Hungary is not a member of the Carpathian Eight regional cooperation initiative launched by President Zelensky, but it is closely following its establishment and further development,” the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs replied on Monday afternoon. They noted that, on the Hungarian side, the event was observed on site by Ádám Ceglédi, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim at the Hungarian Embassy in Kyiv. “Hungary did not sign the declaration adopted at the forum; the joint declaration was adopted by representatives of Ukraine, Austria, Romania, Poland, Serbia, and Slovakia,” they stated. These are the very countries whose representatives appear in the photos and videos shared by the Ukrainian President. Photo: Yurii Rylchuk / Ukrinform / Future Publishing / Getty Images The Ukrainians—at least according to their own account—were surprised by this development and the Hungarian PM's remarks in parliament. “We find the Hungarian Prime Minister’s unnecessarily confrontational statements toward Ukraine surprising,” the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on Monday evening in response to the news. https://www.dw.com/en/europe-to-release-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NfVy Diesel prices have soared since the US waged war against Iran Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP Advertisement US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Europe will release parts of its diesel reserves with immediate effect. "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil ," Trump posted on his Truth Social account, adding that the process will begin "immediately." This comes as the US leader faces growing pressure at home due to mounting prices of oil and other goods as a result of the Iran war and his trade policies. According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of a diesel gallon in the US was 6.37 dollars (5.65 euros). Trump has argued the soaring prices are worth it in order to make sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons, with the prices supposedly coming down after the war's end. Russia's ban on exports, which came due to Ukraine's attacks on its refineries, also contributed to the hit in diesel supply around the world. Macron confirms move French President Emmanuel Macron , who is also the G7 chair, confirmed the news by saying that the G7 will release up to 100 million barrels over the next four months. Macron also committed to refraining from any trade-limiting measures when it comes to petroleum and energy products between partner countries. "Our citizens' concerns about energy prices remain a top priority," G7 leaders said in a joint statement published by Macron. "We will monitor developments closely and stand ready to adjust measures as needed." Diesel prices have also risen sharply in Germany Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance This comes after a call between Macron and Trump on the issue took place overnight, the French Embassy in the US said. The US had demanded France, Germany and other European countries to release 100 million diesel barrels within a 20-day window, Reuters reported, citing sources.
